title: Memorandum of Contract for Real Estate Wholesaling: What It Is and Why You Need One
excerpt: A memorandum of contract is one of the most powerful legal tools a real estate wholesaler can use to protect their deals. Learn exactly how it works, when to file it, and how to use it to stop sellers from backing out or selling to someone else.
author: AIWholesail Team

metaDescription: Learn how a memorandum of contract for real estate wholesaling protects your deals, prevents double-selling, and keeps sellers from backing out before closing.

sections.content: You found a motivated seller, negotiated a great price, and signed a purchase agreement. You're ready to assign the deal and collect your fee. Then the seller calls and says they changed their mind — or worse, they already sold to someone else. This scenario happens more than most new wholesalers expect, and it can cost you thousands of dollars and weeks of wasted time. A memorandum of contract for real estate wholesaling is the legal tool that prevents exactly this from happening.
What Is a Memorandum of Contract?

A memorandum of contract (also called a memorandum of agreement or notice of interest) is a short legal document that gets recorded at the county courthouse after you sign a purchase agreement with a seller. It does not disclose the price or the specific terms of your deal. Instead, it simply gives public notice that a contract exists between you and the seller for a specific property. Once recorded, it creates what is legally known as a 'cloud on title,' which means no title company will allow the property to be sold to anyone else until your contract is resolved.
How It Creates a Cloud on Title

When a memorandum is recorded with the county recorder's office, it becomes part of the public record tied to that property's address and parcel number. Any title search — which every legitimate real estate closing requires — will turn up that memorandum. A title company will not issue a clean title policy if there is an unresolved cloud on title. This means the seller literally cannot complete a sale to another buyer without first dealing with your recorded interest. It is one of the strongest protections available to a wholesaler short of owning the property outright.

Pro Tip: Record your memorandum of contract within 24 to 48 hours of getting the purchase agreement signed. The faster you record it, the better protected you are. Recording fees are typically just $10 to $50 depending on your county — a tiny cost compared to the deal you're protecting.
Why Wholesalers Need This Protection

Motivated sellers are often in stressful financial situations. Divorce, foreclosure, job loss, or estate issues can make them unpredictable. A seller who seemed committed on Tuesday may get cold feet by Friday, especially if a neighbor or family member talks them out of the deal. In competitive markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), sellers may also receive multiple offers after going under contract with you. Without a recorded memorandum, you have little practical recourse if a seller walks away or double-contracts with another buyer.
"A signed contract is only as strong as your ability to enforce it. Recording a memorandum of contract turns a piece of paper into a real legal encumbrance that the whole world can see."
What Goes Into a Memorandum of Contract

The memorandum itself is intentionally brief. It references the existence of the underlying purchase agreement without revealing its financial terms. Most states require it to be notarized before it can be recorded. Here is what a standard memorandum of contract typically includes:

items: Full legal names of the buyer (you or your entity) and the seller
Full legal description of the property (from the deed or county records)
Property address and parcel identification number
The date the purchase agreement was executed
A statement that a valid contract exists between the parties for the sale of the property
The expiration or closing date of the underlying contract (optional but recommended)
Notary acknowledgment section for both parties or just the buyer, depending on state law

sections.content: What It Does NOT Include

You do not need to disclose your purchase price, your assignment fee, your buyer's identity, or any contingencies in the purchase agreement. Keeping the memorandum brief is intentional — you want to protect your deal without revealing how profitable it might be. Sellers who see a large assignment fee in a public document might try to cancel and renegotiate. The memorandum keeps your business private while still giving you legal teeth.
Step-by-Step: How to Record a Memorandum of Contract

items: Step 1 — Get your purchase agreement signed by the seller and make sure it includes a clause giving you permission to record a memorandum or assign the contract.
Step 2 — Pull the full legal description of the property from the county assessor's website or the most recent deed. Do not use just the street address — you need the legal description.
Step 3 — Draft the memorandum using a template approved for your state. Many real estate attorneys sell these for $50 to $150, and it is worth having one reviewed at least once.
Step 4 — Have the document notarized. Most states require the buyer's signature to be notarized, and some require the seller's as well.
Step 5 — Take the notarized memorandum to your county recorder's office or submit it electronically if your county allows it. Pay the recording fee, which typically ranges from $10 to $50.
Step 6 — Keep your certified copy with the recording stamp. This is your proof that the memorandum is on record.

Step 7 — Once your deal closes or the contract expires, file a release of memorandum to clear the title. Failing to do this can damage your relationship with that seller and create problems for future deals.

sections.content: Pro Tip: Always include a clause in your purchase agreement that requires the seller to cooperate with the release of the memorandum after closing or contract termination. This makes it much easier to clear the title quickly and maintain goodwill with the seller.
Common Mistakes Wholesalers Make With Memorandums

Even experienced investors make costly errors with this document. One of the most common is waiting too long to record — some wholesalers file it days or even weeks after signing the purchase agreement, by which point the seller has already found another buyer. Another mistake is using an incorrect legal description, which can make the memorandum unenforceable or fail to show up properly in a title search. Always double-check the legal description against the county's official records before filing.

A third mistake is forgetting to release the memorandum after a deal falls through. A cloud on title that you created but never removed can follow you professionally. Title companies and real estate attorneys in your market will remember if you leave title clouds behind. Always file a release of memorandum promptly, even if you're frustrated that the deal didn't close. Does Every State Allow Memorandums of Contract?

Most states allow wholesalers to record a memorandum of contract, but the rules vary. Some states have specific statutes governing what the document must contain and how it must be formatted to be recordable. A handful of states have seen regulatory pushback on certain wholesaling practices, so it is always smart to work with a local real estate attorney at least once to confirm that your memorandum template complies with your state's recording requirements. The cost of an attorney review — typically $150 to $300 — is insignificant compared to the protection it provides on a $5,000 to $25,000 wholesale fee.
